results.comment: 47:40 I'm a little disappointed with the guest's conflation of gravitational force and gravitational potential. If you had a planet with a large twin that it was tidally locked with, yes, it would shape itself to have a uniform gravitational potential, but that is not equivalent to having the same surface gravity everywhere. The force due to gravity is proportional to the gradient of the gravitational potential, and just because the potential may be the same everywhere along the surface, it doesn't mean the gradient is the same everywhere.  Similarly, the situation with super-earths isn't so much that the surface gravity is so high, but that with a more massive planet, you are likely to be too deep in the gravitational well to be able to escape. You could have, for example, a planet with twice the radius of the Earth and four times the mass. The gravitational acceleration, -G*M/R^2, is the same as on Earth, because -G*M/R^2 == -G*(4M)/(2R)^2. But the gravitational potential, -G*M/R (not squared!) is much lower (i.e., a larger negative number) for the super-earth, so even though you could launch a rocket, and it would look similar to launching it from Earth, you wouldn't be able to burn the engines long enough to climb out of the potential well.  (Source: my masters thesis)
